Looking at the triangle arrangement, the coin centers sit at triangular lattice points: bottom row (0,0), (1,0), (2,0); middle row (0.5, √3/2), (1.5, √3/2); top (1, √3).

The circle (ring) arrangement has centers at the vertices of a regular hexagon with side 1 (each coin touching two neighbors).

**Checking overlap:** If I place the hexagonal ring with vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1.5, √3/2), (1, √3), (0, √3), (−0.5, √3/2), then four triangle coins — (0,0), (1,0), (1.5, √3/2), (1, √3) — already sit in correct ring positions. Moving just the two remaining coins (the bottom-right corner to (0, √3) and the middle-left coin to (−0.5, √3/2)) completes the circle. So 2 moves suffice.

**Why 1 move is impossible:** If only one coin moved, five triangle coins would have to already lie on some hexagonal ring. Any five vertices of a regular hexagon (side 1) have distance multiset {four 1s, four √3s, two 2s}. But every five-coin subset of the triangle has either five or seven pairs at distance 1 — never four. So no five coins of the triangle can lie on a ring.

Therefore the smallest number of coins that must be moved is:

\boxed{2}
